references.text: Parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus says the same words: "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick." This is the direct parallel to Luke's account.
Parallel passage in Mark where Jesus responds with the same statement that it is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. Mark's version of the same event at Levi's calling.
The following verse where Jesus explains the purpose of his statement: "I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." This expands on the meaning of verse 31.
God says through Ezekiel that he will seek out the lost, bring back the exiles, bind up the injured and strengthen the weak. Jesus applies this image to himself as a doctor for the sick.
The Lord invites reconciliation and offers cleansing from sin. Isaiah's call to repentance for sinners reflects Jesus' attitude of seeking those who need salvation.

Hosea urges the people to turn back to the Lord, for he has torn them but will heal them. The image of God as a doctor for his people forms the background for Jesus' statement that the sick need a doctor.
Jesus says that the Son of Man has come to seek and save the lost. This expresses the same principle as in 5:31 — Jesus came for those who need help.
The parable of the lost sheep illustrates the same point: Jesus actively seeks out the lost, just as a doctor seeks out the sick.
Paul confirms that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. This aligns with Jesus' own statement that he came as a doctor for the sick and not for the healthy.
The Messiah is anointed to proclaim good news to the poor, to bind up those who have a broken heart — a prophetic image of Jesus' ministry to the needy and "sick."
